profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting at an industrial equipment manufacturer after three field returns of a servo-driven carton sealing module intermittently failed during customer startup. The issue appeared within two weeks of ECO-417, which introduced a revised cable clamp, a small harness routing change, and a drive firmware update on newly built units. Production is still running, but Quality has asked Engineering to determine whether the dominant failure path is mechanical strain, electrical supply behavior, contamination, or a change-control interaction. The meeting agenda is to compare the available evidence from returns and factory observations, agree on the most credible root-cause hypothesis to test next, and decide on an immediate containment action plus a short reproduction plan. The expected outcome is a shared-seeming plan for what to examine, what to rerun, and what temporary controls to apply before the next shipment window.

members.name: Lena Ortiz
members.expertise: failure analysis, root-cause methods, lab reproduction, field return triage, change analysis
members.background: Lena supports post-release investigations for electro-mechanical packaging equipment and typically works from returned hardware, event logs, teardown findings, and engineering change histories to isolate failure mechanisms that can be defended in a corrective-action review.
members.private_state: She wants a technically rigorous failure narrative before anyone broadens corrective action, and she is concerned the organization will anchor too quickly on the visible ECO change without reproducing the field signature under controlled conditions.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the 'suspect units' or 'problem units,' they naturally mean the three customer-returned sealing modules with documented field faults, not line-side units with one-time alarms.
Reproducing the issue means recreating the same startup fault signature seen in the field logs at least once under instrumented lab conditions, ideally on a returned assembly.
The 'current production batch' is shorthand for the post-ECO-417 configuration population, because that is the meaningful common factor for containment and causal reasoning.
Running the 'startup sequence' for failure analysis implies the cold-start lab protocol with soak time, monitored supply rails, and first-motion capture rather than a routine production power-up.
Unless someone explicitly says otherwise, the returned units still represent the released production firmware state and have not been altered after arrival.

members.name: Marcus Chen
members.expertise: assembly process control, end-of-line test behavior, change rollout, work-instruction implementation, shop-floor containment
members.background: Marcus owns the sealing module assembly cell, monitors process escapes and startup alarms at final test, and coordinated shop-floor implementation of ECO-417, including fixture notes, harness handling guidance, and operator instructions.
members.private_state: He wants to avoid an unnecessary rollback or production disruption, and he is focused on actions technicians can execute immediately on the floor while still appearing responsive to the field issue.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the 'suspect units' or 'problem units,' that naturally includes the three field returns plus the six recent modules that threw startup alarms during final test even though they later passed after reset.

Reproducing the issue means provoking the same controller startup alarm on any relevant unit using the standard end-of-line sequence, because that is the repeatable operational checkpoint available today.
The 'current production batch' means everything physically in WIP, final test, and finished-goods staging right now, since containment has to map to what the line can touch immediately.
Running the 'startup sequence' means using the production test fixture, standard HMI prompts, and normal operator flow because that is the plant's authoritative startup condition.
The ECO-417 firmware update was deployed consistently enough that firmware state does not need separate verification unless there is direct evidence of a loading error.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the suspect population
misalignment_points.surface_form: They refer to the 'suspect units' or 'problem units' as if they mean the same hardware population.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Lena means the three customer-returned sealing modules with field-documented intermittent startup failures now in the reliability lab.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus means those three returns plus six factory-test modules that showed a startup alarm once during final test before passing after reset.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The softer labels 'suspect units' and 'problem units' are routinely used before formal disposition, so neither person expects the phrase to require a precise count; both populations are plausibly related enough that the difference stays invisible during a normal troubleshooting exchange.

misalignment_points.topic: Meaning of reproducing the startup fault
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree they need to 'reproduce the startup fault' before locking the root cause.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Lena requires recreating the same intermittent servo undervoltage or motion-initiation signature seen in the customer event logs, ideally on a returned module under lab instrumentation after cold soak.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus considers any recurrence of the startup controller alarm during the standard end-of-line power-up routine sufficient evidence that the issue has been reproduced.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Reproduce-the-fault language is standard and sounds methodologically aligned, but the evidentiary threshold is a second-order assumption each role imports from daily practice, so the phrase feels specific enough even when it is not.

misalignment_points.topic: Boundary of the immediate containment set
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to put containment on the 'current production batch' while the investigation continues.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Lena assumes this means the post-ECO-417 configuration population, since the point of containment is to bracket the changed design state most likely tied to the field issue.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus assumes this means all units physically on the line, in final test, and in finished-goods staging at the moment, regardless of whether they were built just before or after the ECO cutover.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'current production batch' sounds operationally concrete inside manufacturing settings, but each person silently maps it to the boundary relevant to their own work: configuration-defined population versus physically present inventory.

misalignment_points.topic: Which startup sequence is being rerun
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'run the startup sequence' on the suspect units.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Lena intends the cold-start lab protocol on a returned assembly, including overnight soak, external supply monitoring, and capture of the first servo motion attempt.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus intends the standard production startup sequence at end-of-line using the plant test fixture, normal operator prompts, and immediate rerun capability.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both procedures are legitimately called the startup sequence within the company, and because each is routine in its own context, neither participant experiences the phrase as ambiguous enough to warrant clarification.
